title: Learning discrete-logarithm interval concepts

problem.name: Learning discrete-logarithm interval concepts
problem.statement_latex: For prime $p$, generator $g\in\mathbb F_p^*$, and hidden $s$, let $f_s(x)=+1$ when $\log_gx$ lies in the cyclic interval of $(p-1)/2$ exponents starting at $s$, and $-1$ otherwise. Given uniform classical labeled examples, learn a classifier with error at most $0.01$. Complexity uses gates and training/inference time; $n=\lceil\log_2p\rceil$.

evidence.description_latex: An efficient classical learner with inverse-polynomial prediction advantage would solve discrete logarithms.

hardware.description_latex: Polynomial logical qubits and modular arithmetic; kernel shots and classical support-vector training enter the cost.

quantum.headline_latex: $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time at constant accuracy by support-vector classification with quantum kernel estimation. Kernels are squared overlaps of modular-exponentiation feature states. Alternatively, Shor's algorithm maps examples to exponent intervals for classical learning.

classical.headline_latex: Achieving accuracy $1/2+1/\operatorname{poly}(n)$ gives an efficient classical discrete-logarithm algorithm. A direct attack computes logarithms with the number field sieve and learns the interval, with heuristic time $\exp(O(n^{1/3}(\log n)^{2/3}))$ for prime fields, up to polynomial training overhead.
